They report losses in both ALFWorld and WebShop for greedy replay and other evaluators, and recommend verifying repairs with the executor that will run them. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show evaluator-executor mismatch loses deployment value, measuring greedy replay losses on ALFWorld and WebShop using independent rollouts of the deployed policy.

entry.title: Limits on preparing light states via phase-space majorization
entry.summary: Fundamental limits on photonic state preparation from phase-space majorization arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper studies probabilistic conversions between quantum states of light, deriving fundamental bounds for both exact and approximate transformations. The authors develop a theory of weak, fully relative majorization that compares the disorder of phase-space functions. Focusing on Wigner functions in multimode photonic systems, they establish no-go results and tradeoff relations for conversions involving squeezed, cat, Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill, and Fock states. The work derives novel bounds and recovers known tight ones. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a phase-space relative majorization theory yielding new no-go bounds and tradeoffs for photonic state preparation, recovering known tight bounds.

entry.title: Decorrelating AI Advice Layers to Reduce Synchronized Liquidation in Agentic Wealth Management
entry.summary: Decorrelating the Advice Layer: A Calibrated Fragility Metric and Tested Mitigations for Synchronized Liquidation in Agentic Wealth Management arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper models conversational AI agents that run continuous market analysis, allocation, and execution for wealth management clients, calibrated to model concentration, retail turnover, and 33 years of equity returns. It finds that the effective number of independent decision-makers is bounded, and that synchronized automation rather than model concentration drives market-wide tail losses. A fragility index built from aggregate flow, public returns, and impact estimates forecasts tail liquidation out of sample better than concentration or correlation measures. Dispersing overlay parameters, staging execution, and adding a participation breaker together cut tail liquidation by 63 percent. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose an aggregate-flow fragility index and report that synchronized automation, not model concentration, drives tail liquidation in simulations and historical replays.

entry.title: A differentiable watershed layer for trainable segmentation networks
entry.summary: The Power Watershed as a Differentiable Segmentation Layer arXiv · Oct 28, 2026The paper places a Power Watershed, the limit of a seeded Random Walker as its edge-weight exponent grows, at the end of a segmentation network so it can be trained end to end. The finite-exponent solve is exactly differentiable through one adjoint solve. On PanNuke nuclei segmentation, the layer turns a U-Net into an instance segmenter, raising instance F1 from 0.656 to 0.795. ★★★★ Notable: The authors embed a differentiable Power Watershed layer at the end of a U-Net and report instance F1 rising from 0.656 to 0.795 on PanNuke nuclei segmentation.

entry.title: Similar Scores, Opposite Failures: Human Correction for Video Caption Evaluation
entry.summary: Similar Scores, Opposite Failures: Human Correction as an Instrument for Video Caption Evaluation arXiv · Oct 28, 2026The paper finds that reference-overlap metrics built for single-sentence image captions fail to separate reviewer-accepted from rejected dense video captions, performing near chance. Six frontier models captioned 196 short clips, which trained annotators post-edited against a fixed failure taxonomy, reviewing each caption once as a whole-clip overview and once window by window. Camera and shot errors were flagged about 4.7 times more often in the window-by-window review, and models with similar accuracy showed clearly different failure profiles. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use human post-editing against a fixed taxonomy on 196 clips, reporting window-level review finds 4.7x more camera errors than overview review, while BLEU-4 is near chance at separating ac

entry.title: Predicting the Reward, Not the World: Training Models to Choose Better ML Programs
entry.summary: Predict the Reward, Not the World: World Reward Models for ML Agents arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper proposes World Reward Models (WRMs) for search-based machine-learning agents, which learn directly from real execution results which candidate program will perform better, instead of predicting intermediate execution outcomes. The proposed model, ForeCritic, picks the better program 79.4% of the time on 12,438 held-out pairs from 26 ML tasks, compared with 53% to 62% for general-purpose LLM judges. When integrated into AIDE, ML-Master, and ForeAgent, it cuts mean task time by 4.4 to 7.5 times while keeping mean scores within 0.01 or raising them. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose world reward models that directly select the better candidate program without predicting execution outcomes, report proofs and 12,438 held-out pair evaluations, and test speedups w

entry.title: Masked Erosion: How Acceptance Gates Lose Redundant Safeguards in Self-Improving Agents
entry.summary: Masked Erosion: How Acceptance Gates Lose Redundant Safeguards in Self-Improving Agents arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper studies self-improving LLM agents that edit their own prompts and rules, keeping edits only when an acceptance gate scores them higher on task batches. Because overlapping safeguards mask the effect of deleting one, the gate can approve harmful changes based on task success alone, eroding redundancy unseen. The authors measured harm across all subsets of four safeguards in two environments, running 411 improvement loops under ten gate rules. They also report that evaluation batch size and the statistical test used affect which safeguards are kept. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show acceptance gates erode redundant safeguards via masking, reporting 411 controlled loops and a frozen predictive model.

entry.title: Reliable, scalable, value-aligned generative recommendation for large-scale advertising (GR4AD-X)
entry.summary: Towards Reliable, Scalable, and Value-Aligned Generative Recommendation for Large-Scale Advertising arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper presents GR4AD-X, an advertising recommendation framework for the Kuaishou platform that generates discrete semantic identifiers autoregressively. It improves semantic identifier reliability with Multi-Path assignment, scales model capacity along several dimensions under serving constraints, and aligns generation with commercial value through the UniVGD method. Large-scale online A/B tests on Kuaishou's advertising platform show a 3.07% cumulative revenue gain over the deployed GR4AD baseline while meeting latency and throughput requirements. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose Multi-Path SID assignment, multi-dimensional capacity scaling, and unified value alignment, reporting a 3.07% revenue gain in large-scale Kuaishou online A/B tests.

entry.title: Optimal Regret Bounds for Communication-Efficient Decentralized Online Learning
entry.summary: Optimal Regret for Communication-Efficient Decentralized Online Learning arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper studies decentralized online convex optimization where networked learners minimize a sequence of global losses using only local losses and compressed messages from neighbors. The authors propose Ascent-gossip, which combines an online compression strategy with a Chebyshev recursion to reach consensus faster than existing compressed gossip methods. Using this method, they present an online algorithm whose regret bounds for convex and strongly convex losses match known lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. ★★★★ Notable: The authors combine online compression with Chebyshev recursion, reporting regret bounds matching lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.

entry.title: Game-Theoretic Foundations for Undiscounted Bisimulation Metrics
entry.summary: Game-Theoretic Foundations for Undiscounted Bisimulation Metrics arXiv · Oct 28, 2026Bisimulation metrics measure task-relevant state similarity in reinforcement learning, but existing constructions mostly cover discounted MDPs. This paper reinterprets these metrics as game value functions of zero-sum turn-based games, giving unique definitions for total- and average-reward settings. It also analyzes how metric finiteness depends on MDP structure and shows that the metrics bound total-reward and optimal relative value differences. Error and suboptimality guarantees for aggregation-based planning are provided. ★★★★ Notable: The authors recast bisimulation metrics as zero-sum game values, giving unique definitions for undiscounted total- and average-reward MDPs, with bounds on value differences and aggregation-planning er

entry.title: ParaTTT: Parallelizing Test-Time Training Layers with Deep Memories
entry.summary: ParaTTT: Parallelizing Test-Time Training Layers with Deep Memories arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper introduces ParaTTT (PTTT), an algorithm that parallelizes deep nonlinear memories in test-time training layers by iteratively refining estimates of the inner-loop gradient trajectory. Each refinement uses three chunkwise-parallel passes, and the exact online gradient descent recurrence is a fixed point of the iteration. With two refinement steps at 4K context, the inner-loop evaluation is reported to be 32 times faster than TTT-MLP with block approximation at matched error, and the 340M model trains 4.9 times faster. Models at 340M and 1.3B parameters match or exceed Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2 on language-modeling perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, with better recall than linear recurrences. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose iterative chunkwise-parallel refinement for deep nonlinear test-time training memories, report 340M and 1.3B model comparisons, and give a convergence proof for a two-layer variant

entry.title: Near-optimal regret for adversarial linear bandits under strong corruption
entry.summary: Nearly Minimax Optimal Regret for Adversarial Linear Bandits with Strong Corruptions arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper studies adversarial linear bandits where a strong adversary corrupts observed rewards after seeing the learner's action, within a known total corruption budget C. The authors propose CRW-FTRL, which uses a radius-weighted entropy regularizer and a normalized kernel estimator whose corruption sensitivity depends on per-action radii. The algorithm achieves regret that matches the best corruption-free rate and the corruption lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Applied to discretized general compact action sets, it yields regret of order d√T plus dC. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a radius-weighted regularizer achieving near-minimax regret under strong corruption, matching the corruption-free rate up to logarithmic factors.

entry.title: Disparity Laundering: Consensus Without Fairness in Clinical Multi-Agent AI
entry.summary: Disparity Laundering: Consensus Without Fairness in Clinical Multi-Agent Systems arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper examines demographic bias when clinical large language models operate as multi-agent teams. Testing five model families and four aggregation topologies on 120 MIMIC-IV emergency cases with counterfactual demographic swaps, all configurations preserved the direction of individual agents' answers, giving Black patients more acute triage. The authors report that fairness instructions and demographic masking did not close the gap, while a diverse-perspective ensemble that pools counterfactual versions during deliberation reduced the disparity by 67 to 94%. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce disparity laundering and report a full factorial of five model families and four topologies on 120 MIMIC-IV cases under counterfactual swaps.

entry.title: Is It My Preference? A Role Grounding Attack That Misattributes Preferences in Agent Memory
entry.summary: Is it my preference? Role Grounding Attack against Agent's Memory via Social Interaction arXiv · Oct 28, 2026LLM-based agents share experiences on social platforms and remember new preferences, but existing memory systems can misattribute roles to principals. The paper formalizes the Role Grounding Attack (RGA), which uses nested conversations so that a victim agent records an attacker's preference as the victim user's preference. The authors instantiate RGA as tool selection manipulation and privacy leakage, and evaluate it across five memory systems and six language models. Both attack types achieve high success rates, which the authors argue calls for stronger role grounding. ★★★★ Notable: The authors formalize Role Grounding Attack, exploiting role misattribution in agent memory, and report evaluations across five memory systems and six models for tool manipulation and privacy leakage.

entry.title: Annealed, Averaged Markov Chains Reach the Algorithmic Threshold for Tensor PCA (Part II: Langevin Dynamics)
entry.summary: Averaged Annealed Markov Chains Achieve the Algorithmic Threshold for Tensor PCA, Part II: Langevin Dynamics arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper studies tensor principal components analysis on the sphere, where an unknown vector must be recovered from a noisy observation of its k-th tensor power. The authors show that spherical Langevin dynamics, combined with annealing and ergodic averaging, achieves polynomial-time strong recovery above the algorithmic threshold from a uniformly random initialization. Together with Part I, the results show that local Markov chains can succeed down to the algorithmic threshold from an uninformative cold start. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show annealed, averaged spherical Langevin dynamics recovers tensor PCA signal in polynomial time above the algorithmic threshold from random initialization, continuing Part I.

entry.title: Toffoli gates with no spare qubits, and T-gate counts for Boolean oracles
entry.summary: Ancilla-free randomized Toffoli gates and the T-count of Boolean oracles arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper studies the T-gate cost of Boolean oracles in fault-tolerant Clifford+T circuits. The authors compute sampled parities in place on the gate's own controls, which removes the need for extra qubits once the gate is large enough, using about 8 T gates per bit of precision per random circuit. The same holds for exclusive-ors of affine subspace indicators. The paper also shows that a random set of fixed density needs exponentially many T gates at constant error, whereas an affine subspace of the same density needs a constant number. ★★★★ Notable: The authors remove extra ancilla qubits from the Gosset et al. randomized Toffoli construction, using about 8 T gates per bit of precision, and compare against lower bounds.

entry.title: DecompGym: A Benchmark for LLM Agents Designing Decomposition Algorithms
entry.summary: DecompGym: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Designing Decomposition Algorithms arXiv · Oct 28, 2026The paper introduces DecompGym, a benchmark of 81 optimization instances from nine problem families, including five Benders and four column generation tasks, where agents must write solvers for prescribed decomposition methods. Each solver is checked for running within 60 seconds, numerical feasibility, an LLM judge's audit of the method used, and an objective within 1% of the stored optimum. Evaluating 12 GPT, Claude, and Gemini models over up to ten attempts, the authors find that reflection, which diagnoses failures first, succeeds on 66% of retries versus 39% for independent regeneration. The study concludes that decomposition agents need checks on how a solver reaches its answer, not only output checks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors build a 81-instance benchmark testing LLM agents on Benders and column generation, comparing regeneration with reflection across 12 models, and separating output checks from method audits.

entry.title: Theoretical Limits and Guarantees for Graph-Based Nearest-Neighbor Search
entry.summary: On Worst-Case Guarantees for Graph-Based Nearest-Neighbor Search arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper studies the theoretical guarantees of graph-based nearest neighbor search methods such as HNSW, DiskANN, and NSG, which perform well in practice. The authors prove that standard graph-based methods running greedy search on flat or hierarchical graphs cannot achieve sublinear query time in Euclidean space, even with arbitrarily large approximation factors. They show that allowing Steiner points in the search graph makes sublinear query time possible, with bounds comparable to LSH, and include initial experiments on incorporating Steiner points into practical methods. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove standard graph-based search cannot achieve sublinear query time, and that Steiner points yield LSH-comparable bounds, with initial experiments.

entry.title: What LOL Measures: Hidden Label Shifts in Low-Light Enhancement Benchmarks
entry.summary: What Does LOL Measure? Hidden Label Shifts in Low-Light Enhancement Benchmarks arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper audits the standard low-light image enhancement benchmarks LOL-v1 and LOLv2-Real using 18 public checkpoints from eight methods. It finds that test labels differ from training labels, with LOL-v1 test labels rendered differently and LOLv2-Real test labels darker than its training labels. The authors show that test-set checkpoint selection and released test-time settings affect reported scores and method rankings, and they provide reporting recommendations. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors audit 18 checkpoints of eight methods, report hidden label shifts in LOL benchmarks, and quantify their effect on rankings.

entry.title: Post-training LLMs with LLMON for safer instruction handling
entry.summary: Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper proposes a post-training method using LLMON (LLM Object Notation), which separates executable instructions from passive data and requires identifier-based execution. The authors built a 4.6B-token structured training corpus and post-trained Granite-4.1 3B and 8B base models with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. They report that attack success rates on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks fell from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6% while general capabilities were preserved. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report that LLMON-structured post-training cuts indirect prompt-injection success rates substantially on two Granite models, and introduce attention-based interpretability metrics.

entry.title: SPARSEBLEED: A Hardware Attack Bypassing Privacy Defenses via Sparsity Optimizations
entry.summary: SPARSEBLEED: Bypassing Attribute-Inference Defenses via Sparsity Optimizations arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper presents SparseBleed, a hardware-level attack that infers sensitive input attributes from a single query by exploiting timing signatures of sparsity-driven execution paths in accelerators. It works across Intel AVX2/AVX-512/AMX, NVIDIA Ampere Tensor Cores, and several sparse and dense libraries. The authors evaluate the attack on Texas-100X and compare mitigations, finding that disabling sparsity optimizations is costly while a padding defense adds about 7.24% average overhead. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a hardware-level attribute-stealing attack exploiting sparsity timing, reporting 66.39% Sex inference on Texas-100X and evaluating a padding defense's overhead.

entry.title: Predicting Which Pages AI Answer Engines Cite, with Open Models and a 4B Student
entry.summary: Predicting What Answer Engines Cite: Open Decision Models, Rerankers and a Distilled 4B Student on Ten Engines under Controlled Retrieval arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper studies how to rank candidate web pages by how often answer engines will cite them in generated responses. The authors evaluate pretrained rerankers, a hosted decision model, eight open decision models, and distilled students on GEO-Bench queries across ten engines. A 4B student model fine-tuned from Qwen3-Reranker-4B performs comparably to the strongest scorers, and the model, benchmark, predictions, and code are released. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report comparing rerankers and distilled 4B students against teacher decision models on GEO-Bench across ten answer engines.

entry.title: Vision Tomography: Portable 3D Face-Skull Reconstruction from Visual Data
entry.summary: Vision Tomography: Towards Portable 3D Bidirectional Face-Skull Inference from Visual Data arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper introduces Vision Tomography (VT), a framework that reconstructs paired 3D face and skull geometry from visual inputs such as images or sketches. The authors built a dataset of over 200 cases with CT skulls, CT faces, and textured face scans, and proposed a 3D Bidirectional Face-Skull Morphable Model (BFSM) that infers shape between face and skull via a shared coefficient space. The framework is demonstrated in forensic and medical applications, including paired reconstruction and predicting surgical outcomes through joint face-skull editing. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a bidirectional face-skull morphable model and a 200-plus sample dataset for paired 3D reconstruction from visual data, reporting experiments in forensic and medical applications.

entry.title: How Open-Source Software Adopts Post-Quantum Cryptography: Practices and Challenges
entry.summary: Understanding Post-Quantum Cryptography Adoption: Practices, Challenges, and Evolution in Open-Source Software arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper mines 114,361 commits and 5,713 issues across 179 open-source repositories to study how projects implement and maintain post-quantum cryptography (PQC) support. About 90% of PQC-related commits concern maintenance of existing support, and build, packaging, dependency, and functional failures account for roughly half of the categorized issues. After the 2024 NIST standards were finalized, standardized algorithm names appeared in more than 80% of analyzed PQC changes, but first implementations did not significantly increase. ★★★★ Notable: The authors mine 114,361 commits and 5,713 issues across 179 repositories, building an 11-category taxonomy of PQC challenges and releasing the dataset and pipeline.

entry.title: Random Centres and the ε-Dependence of Constant-Round Planar Domination
entry.summary: Random Centres and the ǎrepsilon-Dependence of Constant-Round Planar Domination arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper studies constant-round LOCAL algorithms for minimum dominating set on planar graphs. It replaces the heaviest-edge star selection in the clustering step with a random-centre rule, which reduces the round-complexity exponent. The authors also analyse how the approximation parameter ε affects the number of rounds, showing Ω(1/ε) rounds are needed on paths and Θ(1/ε) rounds are optimal on forests and outerplanar graphs. ★★★★ Notable: Replaces heaviest-edge star selection with random centres, reducing the planar round exponent from about 25.81 to below 5.89, with lower bounds reported.

entry.title: Who Else Is In? How AI Agents Might Start Secret Collusion Using Vague Messages
entry.summary: Who Else Is In? The authors run a mutual identification game in which two agents must recognize each other while solving a shared task, and some models succeed without explicit guidance, often evading monitors at low false positive rates. They report that as messages grow more indirect, monitor punishment can fall faster than partner coordination, creating a profitable middle ground. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a mutual identification game showing strategic vagueness can initiate collusion past monitors; the abstract reports successful handshakes and an asymmetric monitor-punishment ver

entry.title: Encore: Turning Public Exploit PoCs into Threat Hunting Rules
entry.summary: Set an Exploit to Catch an Exploit: Compiling Public Proofs of Concept into Threat Hunting Rules arXiv · Oct 28, 2026The paper observes that public exploit code for new vulnerabilities usually appears before detection rules for their exploitation. The authors present Encore, which compiles a public Python proof-of-concept exploit into CVE-specific hunting rules over a web service's existing logs, without running the code. The paper reports that Encore's rules find 43 of 45 evaluated CVEs, separate exploit payloads from harmless matched requests, and raise no alerts across 27,081 legitimate and crawl requests. ★★★★ Notable: The authors compile public PoC exploits into hunting rules without execution, reporting results on 45 CVEs against Splunk's public attack data.

entry.title: Human-Residual Steering: Aligning Frozen LLM Judges with Human Judgment Distributions
entry.summary: Human-Residual Steering: Aligning Frozen LLM Judges with Human Judgment Distributions arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper proposes Human-Residual Steering (HRS), a method that aligns frozen large language model judges with the distribution of individual human ratings by learning hidden-state interventions. Across 14 benchmarks and four judges from three model families, HRS outperforms all evaluated frozen-weight baselines on distribution matching. It also trains about 88 times fewer parameters than distributional fine-tuning. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose learned hidden-state interventions to align frozen LLM judges with human distributions, reporting gains across 14 benchmarks with far fewer trained parameters.

entry.title: Finite-Sample Optimal Conformal Prediction Sets under Covariate Shift
entry.summary: Finite-Sample Optimal Conformal Prediction Sets under Covariate Shift arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper studies conformal prediction under covariate shift when the covariate density ratio is known, aiming for prediction sets with minimal expected length under the target distribution. For every calibration sample size, the authors prove that combining an inverse conditional-density score with randomized weighted conformal calibration minimizes expected length among all rules valid over the weighted-exchangeability class. They approximate the oracle with quantile and kernel histograms, including forest-weighted estimators, and select estimators and tuning parameters by resampling. Experiments on 36 known-density configurations and four public regression datasets compare coverage, set length, and runtime with existing methods. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove the inverse-density score with randomized weighted calibration minimizes expected set length over weighted-exchangeable rules, and report experiments on 36 density configurations and

entry.title: Lower bound for projection-free online learning with linear oracles
entry.summary: An Ω(T³/4) lower bound for projection-free online learning with linear minimization oracles arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper studies projection-free online learning algorithms that handle the decision set using linear minimization oracles. Prior work showed that Online Frank-Wolfe achieves regret scaling as T^{3/4} under specific tunings, but whether all tunings do so was open. The authors prove a universal worst-case regret lower bound of Ω(T^{3/4} m^{-1/4}) for any projection-free algorithm making at most m oracle calls per round. They also propose an extended Online Frank-Wolfe that uses multiple linear optimizations per round and prove a regret upper bound of O(max{T^{3/4} m^{-1/4}, √T}). ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove a universal regret lower bound for projection-free algorithms and match it with an extended OFW upper bound, answering an open question.

entry.title: Early Signs of Feature Learning in Deep Linear Networks
entry.summary: Investigating the Early Signatures of Feature Learning in Deep Linear Networks arXiv · Oct 28, 2026The paper analyzes features learned by a deep linear network in a mean-field parameterization after a single gradient step from initialization, using high-dimensional data with a low-dimensional spiked signal. It derives closed-form expressions for the bias, variance, and generalization error of kernel ridge regression on these features. A one-step generalization advantage appears only when spike strength and effective signal-to-noise ratio are sufficiently large, and it vanishes for isotropic inputs. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a closed-form account of one-step feature learning in mean-field deep linear networks and derive bias, variance, and generalization error expressions.

entry.title: Measuring Where Intent Is Lost When AI Agents Write Smart Contracts
entry.summary: Measuring Where Intent Gets Lost in Agentic Smart Contract Synthesis arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper examines whether AI agents that write smart contracts from plain-English descriptions actually produce code that behaves as requested. The authors compare an AI-written contract with the original on the same transactions and find that common AI judges and standard analysis tools miss obvious mistakes. They propose asking the client clarifying questions before code generation and checking the result against an independently written executable answer key, which they report works far better than reviewing or patching afterwards. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose asking clarifying questions before generation and checking against an independent executable answer key, reporting results on 600 tasks across three models and releasing tools.

entry.title: Choosing Random Mixtures of AI Versions with Fewest Stakeholder Rejections
entry.summary: Learning Lotteries with Minimal Stakeholder Violations from Membership Queries arXiv · Oct 28, 2026The paper studies how to pick a randomized mixture of several candidate AI system versions that the fewest stakeholders reject. Each stakeholder accepts only mixtures inside an unknown halfspace, and the developer can learn this only by asking yes-or-no membership queries. The authors show that minimizing rejections is APX-hard in general, give exact algorithms for special cases, and provide approximation guarantees when only some stakeholders can be queried. ★★★★ Notable: The authors model stakeholder acceptance as unknown halfspaces, prove APX-hardness for minimizing rejections, and give polynomial and quasi-polynomial exact algorithms with sampling guarantees, plus s

entry.title: TACOS: Terrain-aware contact supervision method for visual footstep planning
entry.summary: TACOS: Terrain-Aware COntact Supervision for Visual Footstep Planning arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper presents TACOS, a method that builds a footstep instability score from the residual of a factor graph used in legged robot state estimation, then projects that score onto earlier camera images to train a dense visual predictor. It proposes a hard score that uses hindsight and a causal soft score available immediately. On 1716 manually annotated contacts and three outdoor test runs, both variants outperform the compared alternatives at detecting instability and ranking its severity. In a real-world 50 m forest trial, the trained predictor handles mud and vegetation and steps around fallen branches. ★★★★ Notable: The authors derive a footstep instability score from factor-graph residuals to supervise a visual predictor, compared against baselines on 1716 annotated contacts and outdoor runs.

entry.title: WebAnything: Automatically Building Reusable Web Environments from Real Sites for AI Agents
entry.summary: WebAnything: From the Wild Web to Scalable Agent Environments arXiv · Oct 28, 2026WebAnything is a framework that automatically rebuilds reusable, resettable website environments from real URLs, so web agents can be trained and tested without manual per-site setup. It constructed 244 website environments across 14 application domains, supporting 12,984 executed and accepted tasks. In a blind audit it outperformed the human-assisted WebHarbor on three fidelity metrics. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on 5,856 interaction trajectories improved success rates on several benchmarks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors automate reconstruction of reusable web environments from real URLs with an independent verifier, reporting 244 sites and gains from fine-tuning on 5,856 trajectories.

entry.title: Backdoors in AI agents planted through poisoned pretraining data
entry.summary: Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning arXiv · Oct 28, 2026The authors pretrained Qwen3 models from scratch at 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B sizes, then post-trained each into a command-line agent. They show that poisoning just 0.1% of the pretraining corpus can implant a backdoor that makes the agent execute attacker-chosen commands on a user's machine when a trigger is present, while behaving normally otherwise. Attack success rate rises with model size, reaching about 92% for the 4B model at a 0.1% poison rate, and remains positive even at 0.0005%. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors show pretraining poisoning can implant a remote code execution backdoor in agents, reporting about 92% attack success for a 4B Qwen3 model at a 0.1% poison rate.

entry.title: When Skills Tell Agents Not to Ask: A Study of Oversight-Loosening Directives in AI Agent Skills
entry.summary: When Skills Tell Agents Not to Ask: A Large-Scale Study of Oversight Directives in Agent Skills arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper studies oversight-loosening directives in agent skills, reusable instruction packages built around a SKILL.md file, such as instructions to proceed without approval or to bypass checks with --no-verify. The authors analyzed 1.53 million English skills from GitSkills, hand-labeled 2,097 units, and trained a detector to scale the analysis. About one in seventeen skills contains such a directive, and skills that run shell code, install packages, or use sudo are more likely to contain one. Existing open-source scanners catch at most 46% of these directives with low precision. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors present the first large-scale study of oversight-loosening directives, analyzing 1.53 million skills, hand-labeling 2,097 units, and training a detector to scale.

entry.title: FVH-Bench: A Benchmark for Image Generator Safety Beyond Obviously Harmful Pictures
entry.summary: FVH-Bench: Evaluating Image Generator Safety Beyond Overtly Harmful Imagery arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper defines functional visual harm (FVH) as the risk from what generated images enable, such as instructions or deceptive artifacts, rather than only what they depict. The authors introduce FVH-Bench, which contains 669 prompts covering five harmful visual functions and ten risk domains. Evaluation of 11 image generators found they rarely refuse these requests and often produce artifacts that fulfill the harmful functions. Existing safety detectors also show limited coverage of FVH. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose functional visual harm and a 669-prompt benchmark, evaluating 11 image generators and existing safety detectors beyond overtly harmful content.

entry.title: How much a weight update changes a model, compared across training stages
entry.summary: What a Weight Update Buys: Leverage Across Training Stages arXiv · Oct 27, 2026The paper introduces leverage, a measure of how much a unit of weight change affects a language model's behavior, and applies it to released Olmo-3, Tülu-3, Zephyr, and OLMo-2 checkpoints. It finds that pretraining updates act like random directions on prose, while SFT, RL, and DPO stages show much higher leverage, up to about 23,000 for DPO. The authors also study how training precision and DARE random drop-and-rescale affect these measurements. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce leverage, a Fisher-form measure of weight update effect, comparing training stages across released checkpoints and deriving a DARE reuse law.

entry.title: Relevance-guided residual calibration for compressing dense retrieval embeddings
entry.summary: Relevance-Guided Residual Calibration for Spectral Compression of Dense Retrieval Embeddings arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper addresses spectral compression of dense retrieval embeddings, noting that existing corpus-derived weighting rules do not account for each retained direction's contribution to relevance. The authors propose Relevance-Guided Residual Calibration (RRC), a closed-form method that uses relevance judgments to refine spectral weights while preserving the compressor's overall trend. Experiments on nine datasets report that SpecTemp combined with RRC achieves the highest mean effectiveness among tested compressors on BEIR and BRIGHT, and the gains persist under scalar and product quantization. ★★★★ Notable: The authors add relevance-guided per-direction residual calibration to spectral compression, reporting gains over SpecTemp on nine BEIR and BRIGHT datasets.

entry.title: Network Structure Doesn't Matter: Classical Consensus Theory Fails for LLM Groups
entry.summary: Network Topology Does Not Matter: The Breakdown of Classical Consensus in LLM Populations arXiv · Oct 25, 2026This paper studies how networks of multiple large language models reach collective agreement. Using eight instruction-tuned models and 73,080 controlled exchanges, the authors measure the models' update behavior and find that they often update outside the range of observed opinions and show active repulsion through negative weights. In simulations of 10,000 agents, network connectivity explains almost none of the outcome variance, while the models' internal update bias and message framing largely govern population dynamics. The authors conclude that classical graph-theoretic metrics are inadequate for LLM populations. ★★★★ Notable: The authors challenge classical consensus assumptions, measure LLM update operators empirically, and report simulations of 10,000 agents.

entry.title: Private information retrieval analyzed through probabilistic inference
entry.summary: PIR through the Lens of Probabilistic Inference IACR ePrint · Oct 29, 2026Private Information Retrieval (PIR) lets a client fetch a database entry without servers learning which index was requested. The paper shows that each server's computation in classic PIR protocols amounts to computing a marginal probability of a product distribution, so efficient exact inference algorithms yield faster server computation. It gives improved server algorithms for several structured function classes and, under the randomized Circuit Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, proves that substantially sublinear server computation cannot be achieved uniformly for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits. ★★★★ Notable: The authors connect each server's computation in classic PIR protocols to marginal inference on a product distribution, yielding faster server algorithms for read-once formulas, bounded-treewidth mode

It also proposes protocols that exploit the asymmetry between minting and forging Keccak bridges, whose end-to-end security is stated to remain open. ★★★★ Notable: The authors generalize capacity loops to arbitrary capacity values and k-block cycles, giving Joux-style multicollisions whose search cost is independent of k. entry.title: Shor's algorithm on cat qubits: estimated resources to factor RSA-2048
entry.summary: Shor's algorithm compiled on cat qubits: 22 593 qubits for RSA-2048 in 3.14 days IACR ePrint · Oct 28, 2026This paper presents an end-to-end resource estimate of Shor's algorithm on superconducting cat qubits, covering RSA, ECDLP and FFDLP. It compiles the main subroutines to physical-qubit operations on repetition-cat-code and LDPC-cat-code architectures and proposes chip layouts and schedules. Under stated assumptions, factoring RSA-2048 is estimated to require about 23,000 cat qubits and 3.14 days, while solving ECDLP on secp256k1 needs at most 30,000 cat qubits and 1 hour. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors present an end-to-end resource estimate of Shor's algorithm on cat qubits, giving chip layouts for RSA-2048, ECDLP and FFDLP and a new parity-Cnot gate.

entry.title: Barriers to Identity-Based Encryption in Generic Group-Action Models
entry.summary: Barriers to Identity-Based Encryption in Generic Group-Action Models IACR ePrint · Oct 28, 2026This paper studies whether identity-based encryption (IBE) can be built from the basic interface of generic cryptographic group actions. In the type-safe generic group-action model, the authors prove that an IBE scheme whose public parameters contain n non-origin action-set element-handles can support at most n identities, and they show a matching construction that makes this bound tight. The result is extended to random-representation models and to actions with an inversion-like twist, suggesting IBE may require extra algebraic structure or non-black-box techniques. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report the first tight lower bounds for IBE in generic group-action models, bounding identities by public parameter size with a matching construction.

entry.title: Faster complete formulas and their application to curves with efficient endomorphisms
entry.summary: Faster complete formulas and their application to curves with efficient endomorphisms IACR ePrint · Oct 29, 2026The paper revisits scalar multiplication on prime curves y² = x³ + b with p ≡ 1 (mod 3), a family that includes secp256k1, BN, and BLS curves. It applies a 15-year-old technique in a new way to reduce the best complete addition from 12 to 11 multiplications. Implemented in libsecp256k1, this yields a 5.2% improvement in constant-time fixed-base scalar multiplication. ★★★★ Notable: The authors apply a 15-year-old technique to cut complete addition to 11 multiplications and propose a complete tripling formula with exception-free τ-NAF; reported on secp256k1 and BLS curves.

entry.title: An algebraic data structure for fast polynomial evaluation over large-characteristic fields
entry.summary: An Algebraic Polynomial Evaluation Datastructure for Fields of Large Characteristic IACR ePrint · Oct 29, 2026This paper studies data structures that evaluate a multivariate polynomial at any input point by using random access to a precomputed encoding of the polynomial. The authors construct algebraic curves over prime fields by using the base-β representation of prime field elements, reducing evaluation recursively to points in boxes of decreasing size. The resulting structure greatly improves the dependence of query complexity on the characteristic p and removes p from the data structure size. The variant of the results is enough to disprove Miltersen's conjecture for all finite fields. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose base-β curve constructions improving query complexity's p-dependence from p^O(1) to d^{O(log log p)}, plus a matching-exponent lower bound.

entry.title: Radical isogeny computation on curves in many models
entry.summary: Radical isogenies on every model IACR ePrint · Oct 28, 2026This paper studies radical isogeny formulae, which compute a cyclic chain of N-isogenies using one N-th root per step without sampling torsion points. Previously, such formulae for general N were known only in Tate normal form. The authors give radical steps of odd degree N on many curve models, including Montgomery and twisted Edwards curves, and report exact operation counts for each model. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend radical isogeny formulas from Tate normal form to many curve models, giving explicit steps for each odd degree with exact operation counts and reported costs.

entry.title: Quantum lower bounds for multi-collisions in bounded-type functions
entry.summary: Quantum Multi-Collision Lower Bounds for Arbitrary Bounded Types IACR ePrint · Oct 28, 2026This paper studies quantum collision finding for functions of a prescribed exact type. The authors prove that finding r-collisions across ℓ distinct equality classes has worst-case bounded-error quantum query complexity Θ_{k,r}(ℓ^{2^{r-1}/(2^r-1)} N^{(2^{r-1}-1)/(2^r-1)}), uniformly over all feasible alphabet sizes q≥n. entry.title: Recovering Falcon Private Keys by Combining Sampler Side-Channel Leakages
entry.summary: Falcon Key Recovery from Joint Sampler Leakages IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026Falcon and the FN-DSA standard based on it create signatures using discrete Gaussian sampling, and power consumption during this step leaks information about secret-dependent values. The paper presents a key-recovery method that combines three observations from each sampler call and turns the resulting candidate sets into constraints on the secret key, solved by regression and integer reconstruction without lattice reduction like LLL or BKZ. The attack recovers all 50 evaluation keys on PQClean Falcon-512 and still recovers 38 of 50 keys on c-fn-dsa, showing that instruction-level normalization alone is insufficient. ★★★★★ Notable: Fuses three sampler side-channel observations to recover Falcon keys without LLL/BKZ; the abstract reports recovering all 50 evaluation keys on Cortex-M4 with a median of 11 signatures.

entry.title: Poly2MsgLeaks: Certified Key Recovery via Polynomial-to-Message Power Leakage
entry.summary: Poly2MsgLeaks: Certified Key Recovery from Polynomial-to-Message Leakage IACR ePrint · Oct 27, 2026This paper presents Poly2MsgLeaks, a profiled chosen-ciphertext power-analysis attack that recovers the full 512-coefficient secret key of the SMAUG-T public-key encryption scheme in its TiMER parameter set. Against single-write message assembly and a two-share masked P2M implementation, the evaluated six-execution attack recovers no complete secret. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors present a profiled P2M chosen-ciphertext power attack on SMAUG-T (TiMER set), report full recovery of the 512-coefficient secret, and give a bound on incorrect key acceptance under a unifo

entry.summary: Mediated Interactions between Fermi Polarons in the Strongly Interacting Regime arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper studies mediated interactions between quasiparticles emerging from a Fermi sea, known as Fermi polarons, using zero-temperature quantum Monte Carlo methods. The main result is that the Landau interaction between polarons stays repulsive across all coupling strengths on the polaronic branch in the strongly interacting regime. entry.title: Can Discrete Tokens Represent Images Without Semantic Loss? This paper tests whether quantizing visual signals into discrete tokens loses meaning, and proposes a new quantization method.
entry.summary: Can Discrete Tokens Serve as Semantically Lossless Representations of Visual Signals? arXiv · Oct 28, 2026The paper challenges the assumption that quantization error inevitably causes semantic loss, finding that discrete representations with larger errors can sometimes understand better. The effective bit budget of discrete indices is identified as the key factor. The authors propose Factorized Vector Quantization, which uses symmetric parallel codebooks to quantize complementary views of visual features, continuing to improve at larger bit budgets. The model reaches state-of-the-art results among discrete-representation models and is competitive with continuous models such as Qwen3-VL, including on fine-grained OCR. ★★★★ Notable: Revisits the claim that quantization error inevitably loses semantics; proposes Factorized Vector Quantization, which the abstract reports matches continuous representations in multimodal understandin

entry.title: When to Intervene at Test Time: PORTAL, a Controller for Timing Interventions and Label Queries
entry.summary: When Should We Intervene at Test Time? arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper studies test-time adaptation, where a deployed model's intervention can help some input batches and hurt others. The authors propose PORTAL, a controller that decides when to deploy an intervention, which inputs to label, and when to stop querying labels. Experiments show that it turns an intervention that lowers overall accuracy into a useful choice on selected batches and prevents severe failures from changes in arrival order. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes PORTAL, a controller that decides when to apply a test-time intervention, which inputs to label, and when to stop querying; each label scores all candidate rules at once, and the abstract rep

entry.summary: Classical Verification of Quantum Computation Beyond the Polynomial Hierarchy arXiv · Oct 28, 2026The paper studies whether a classical polynomial-time verifier can check arbitrary quantum polynomial-time computations without computational assumptions. Relative to a classical oracle, it constructs a language outside the polynomial hierarchy that is exactly decidable in quantum polynomial time, with a public-coin protocol having perfect completeness and soundness error at most 1/4. entry.summary: Timestral arXiv · Oct 28, 2026This paper introduces Timestral, four time series foundation models with 5M to 209M parameters for probabilistic forecasting. entry.summary: Measurement incompatibility and noiseless quantum codes arXiv · Oct 27, 2026The paper studies when a quantum channel universally preserves the incompatibility of measurements. The authors construct a rank-one minimal informationally complete measurement and prove that such preservation holds if and only if the input space contains a noiseless code subspace of full output dimension. They also give an explicit construction of exact encodings and connect the results to quantum steering and quantum error correction. ★★★★ Notable: The authors construct a rank-one MIC with invertible dual operator and claim that a channel universally preserves measurement incompatibility iff its input space contains a full-output-dimension noise

entry.title: Quantum key distribution secured by a bound on information leakage
entry.summary: Prepare-and-measure quantum key distribution from a bound on information leakage arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper examines whether, in prepare-and-measure quantum key distribution, a single bound on information leakage from the sender's source can replace a detailed model of the source. The authors show that this bound, quantified by the probability of guessing the input from everything the source emits, suffices to prove security against collective attacks, with no assumptions on the form, dimension, energy or purity of the emitted states. They note that the standard B92 and BB84 protocols cannot certify a key under this assumption, whereas closely related protocols can reach one secret bit per round in the ideal limit. For noisy implementations, key rates are computed with semidefinite programming relaxations, and the best protocols tolerate visibilities down to 0.84, corresponding to an 8% quantum bit error rate, versus the 11% threshold of device-dependent BB84. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes security proofs from only a sender-side leakage bound, without modeling the source; the authors report one key bit per round ideally and tolerance down to visibility 0.84.

entry.summary: Coherent Optical Control of a Single Donor Electron Spin arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper demonstrates optical initialization, coherent control, and readout of a single donor-bound electron spin in ZnSe. entry.title: Following Gradients to Find Training Data That Erodes Model Safety

entry.summary: SecDMP: Provably Secure Data Memory-Dependent Prefetching (Extended Version) arXiv · Oct 28, 2026Data memory-dependent prefetchers (DMPs) are a CPU optimization in recent mainstream processors that can improve performance but may leak secrets through side channels. The paper classifies DMP leakage, categorizes existing and new attacks, and validates the analysis by implementing open-source DMPs on a RISC-V processor. It proposes SecDMP, a hardware defense in which secrets are marked in memory so DMPs never encode them in the microarchitecture. The authors formally prove SecDMP adds no leakage beyond a baseline without DMPs. ★★★★★ Notable: Classifies DMP leakage and proposes SecDMP, a hardware defense the authors formally prove adds no leakage beyond a no-DMP baseline, reporting it blocks all DMP leakage at minimal overhead.

It also introduces HARP, which allocates ranks per layer from the Hankel spectrum and protects retrieval-sensitive layers. With HARP, halving the state dimension raises average WikiText-2 perplexity by 0.3 points (1.8%) across 130M to 2.7B models, compared with 1.6 points (9.3%) for GHOST. ★★★★ Notable: The authors argue Mamba-2 state compression should target the write-read subspace, proposing balanced truncation plus Hankel-spectrum layer-wise rank allocation (HARP); they report a 0.3-point WikiTex

entry.title: Learning from Points and Patches: A Pre-trained Transformer for Time Series Analysis
entry.summary: Learning from Points and Patches: A Pre-trained Hybrid Attention Transformer for Time Series Analysis arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper presents TimeHAT, a general-purpose pre-training framework for time-series analysis. It introduces a unified point-patch masking strategy that combines point-level and patch-level supervision for contextual reconstruction and causal extrapolation, along with a hybrid attention encoder intended to preserve contextual interactions while mitigating rank degeneration. The model is evaluated on real-world datasets across classification, long-term forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection, under fine-tuning, few-shot, and zero-shot settings, with competitive results reported. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose TimeHAT, combining unified point-patch masking with a hybrid attention encoder, and report competitive results on four downstream tasks across fine-tuning, few-shot, and zero-shot

entry.title: Can AI scientists tell what is truly new?
entry.summary: Do AI Scientists Know What's New? arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper examines how AI scientific discovery pipelines can determine whether a generated research idea is meaningfully novel. The authors build an evaluation framework with temporal ground truth, using four datasets of 1,060 proposals drawn from published papers, reviewer disputes, and ideas later realized by researchers. They introduce ClaimNov, a fine-grained, interpretable claim-level novelty module, which catches 97% of disguised papers at a 1.5% false-alarm rate. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes ClaimNov, a claim-level novelty checker, audited on 1,060 proposals; the authors report it keeps proposals built on prior contributions better than existing checks.

entry.title: Learning-Augmented Coordination Mechanisms: Using Demand Predictions to Improve Equilibrium Efficiency in Congestion Games
entry.summary: Learning-Augmented Coordination Mechanisms arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper studies how selfish behavior reduces efficiency in decentralized resource allocation. It proposes learning-augmented coordination mechanisms that use a possibly inaccurate demand prediction to modify resource costs, with a confidence parameter β that yields near-optimal performance when predictions are accurate while keeping a good worst-case equilibrium guarantee. The paper also gives robustness bounds and impossibility results, including limits on error tolerance in non-atomic games. ★★★★ Notable: Introduces learning-augmented coordination mechanisms for congestion games, aiming for near-optimal performance under accurate predictions while retaining PoS guarantees, with impossibility results.

entry.title: SO-101 Bench: A Simulation Benchmark for Spatial Robot Arm Manipulation
entry.summary: SO-101 Bench: Accessible Spatial Manipulation arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper presents SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-instructed spatial manipulation on the low-cost SO-101 robot arm, built on an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real setup. It includes four tasks, 138 objects, 916 evaluation episodes, and 3,629 simulated demonstrations. Policy rankings in simulation match those on the physical robot, though simulation overestimates success rates. The best learned policies reach about 61%, while an LLM agent that writes code and delegates grasping to a learned policy reaches 83.2%. ★★★★ Notable: Introduces SO-101 Bench, a simulated spatial manipulation benchmark; the authors report five policies keep identical rankings on the real arm (Spearman rho = 1.00).

entry.title: kw-bench: A benchmark testing AI coding harnesses on real investigative accounting tasks
entry.summary: kw-bench: Breaking Frontier Harnesses on Real-World Tasks arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper introduces kw-bench, a benchmark built from real audit, tax and similar engagements described by specialists. Its first task reconstructs five years of VAT records from raw extracts across three generations of SAP systems, graded deterministically without an LLM judge. On the same model, two independent harnesses scored about 0.53 to 0.54, while two lab harnesses scored 0. On a frontier model, two harnesses finished in roughly 22 to 25 minutes with near-perfect scores. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes kw-bench, an investigative benchmark from real audits graded deterministically; OpenCode scored 0.542 and micro-cc 0.528, while the two lab harnesses scored 0.00 off their home model.

entry.title: SOMA: A benchmark testing AI on fine-grained body motion from first-person video
entry.summary: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper introduces SOMA, a benchmark of 1,632 human-verified questions for understanding body motion from egocentric video, covering body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. Thirty-seven multimodal models were evaluated, with humans reaching 68.5% accuracy and the best model, Qwen3.6-27B, reaching 50.0% zero-shot. The authors also release a training dataset and a multimodal baseline aimed at closing this gap. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose SOMA, a fine-grained egocentric body-motion benchmark with 1,632 questions; they report humans at 68.5% versus 50.0% for the strongest MLLM across 37 models, plus error analysis.

entry.title: HELICS: Generating Synthetic Genomes at Biobank Scale with Latent Flow Matching
entry.summary: HELICS: Biobank-scale Conditional Synthetic Genome Generation via Latent Flow Matching arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper presents HELICS, a framework for generating synthetic genome-wide SNP-level genotype data from biobank-scale datasets without requiring haplotype phasing. It compresses over 600K SNPs per genome into 4,096 latent tokens using convolutional autoencoders, then models them with a transformer-based conditional flow matching model. Trained on over 417K UK Biobank genomes, it better preserves real allele frequencies and SNP correlation structure than existing haplotype-based simulators, and can be conditioned on ancestry and genetic liability. ★★★★ Notable: HELICS uses latent flow matching for phasing-free conditional SNP generation on 417K UK Biobank genomes; the authors report higher allele-frequency and correlation fidelity than existing simulators.

entry.summary: CrowdCC: Jointly Benchmarking Corruption Robustness and Deployment Quantization in Crowd Counting arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper introduces CrowdCC, a benchmark that tests crowd-counting models against 23 deployment-motivated image corruptions at three severity levels, while also comparing FP32, FP16, and INT8 precision. It covers four crowd-counting datasets and 26 models, with throughput and energy measured on Jetson Orin NX hardware. entry.title: A dual-objective model that decides which rental listings get instant booking
entry.summary: A Smart Instant Book Filter Model based on Dual-Objective Optimization arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper proposes a smart instant book filter system for hospitality marketplaces, deciding which listings in search results receive instant booking. The system aims to increase the instant book rate while keeping the overall booking rate from decreasing, a dual-objective optimization problem. A/B tests with global users show it outperforms previous human-expert-tuned models on both instant book rate and overall booking rate. The system has been deployed to production and serves millions of users daily. ★★★★ Notable: Proposes a smart instant book filter maximizing instant book rate under a no-drop booking-rate constraint; the authors report global A/B tests beating expert-tuned models, deployed to millions.

entry.title: Algorithm guaranteeing baseline protection and robust performance across adversarial and stochastic settings
entry.summary: Three Worlds for the Price of a Logarithm: Baseline-Protected Best-of-Both-Worlds Combinatorial Semi-Bandits arXiv · Oct 27, 2026The paper proposes DUET, a horizon-free phased mixing algorithm for combinatorial semi-bandits with arbitrary finite action sets. Two observable tests decide when to double the learning weight and when to double the empirical-regret budget and restart. Assuming the baseline selects every arm with positive probability, expected regret relative to the baseline stays logarithmic in T. Regret to any fixed action is Õ(√T) under non-anticipating adversarial losses and polylogarithmic and gap-dependent under i.i.d. losses with a unique optimal action. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose DUET, a horizon-free phased mixing scheme for combinatorial semi-bandits, reporting baseline protection, adversarial and stochastic regret bounds at the cost of a logarithm.

entry.title: Explicit Reed-Solomon codes with optimal list and line decoding
entry.summary: Explicit Reed-Solomon Subspace Designs: Optimal List and Line Decoding arXiv · Oct 27, 2026The paper constructs explicit Reed-Solomon codes over extension fields that can be list-decoded from a fraction 1-R-ε of errors with optimal list size O((1-R)/ε). A simpler strongly explicit evaluation-point construction achieves list size (1/ε)^O(1/ε). Both constructions admit deterministic list-decoding algorithms running in polynomial time. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors give explicit Reed-Solomon codes with near-optimal constant list size via subspace designs, and report a new reduction yielding line decoding and proximity results.

entry.title: count-catcher: Turning model counting certificates into Lean theorems
entry.summary: count-catcher: Lean Theorems from Model Counting Certificates arXiv · Oct 27, 2026The paper presents count-catcher, a tool that converts a CPOG certificate from the exact model counter d4 into a Lean theorem stating that a CNF formula has exactly N models over V variables. With an encoding lemma, this becomes a theorem about the number of combinatorial objects. The authors combine these results with Mathlib and prove the number of Latin squares of order 8 as a weighted sum of hundreds of certified counts drawn from about eight terabytes of certificates. ★★★★ Notable: Turns model counting certificates into Lean theorems; the authors prove the number of order-8 Latin squares and report that CPOG's unverified checker gave wrong counts.

Minimax-optimal small-loss bounds for online linear optimisation on ℓp balls
entry.summary: Minimax-Optimal Small-Loss Bounds for Online Linear Optimisation on ℓ_p Balls arXiv · Oct 27, 2026The paper studies full-information online linear optimisation over the unit ℓp ball for fixed p between 2 and infinity. It presents a follow-the-regularised-leader algorithm whose regret depends on the cumulative excess loss and the dimension, and shows this rate is minimax-optimal for each fixed p. It also analyses a switching extension that keeps the sharp constant, and computes the exact log T coefficient of expected regret for i.i.d. losses. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a small-loss regret bound for online linear optimisation on ℓp balls, reporting that it matches minimax lower bounds with a constant optimal as p→∞, and analyse paths where FTL fails.
